question: What is the primary focus of neurological nursing?

options.A: Managing surgical procedures on the gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Treating chronic lung and respiratory infections
options.C: Monitoring and caring for clients with nervous system disorders
options.D: Providing long-term physical therapy for broken bones

explanation: Neurological nursing centers entirely on assessing, monitoring, and supporting clients experiencing problems with the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h1)

question: Why must nurses monitor clients with neurological problems so closely?

options.A: Hospital insurance policies require hourly doctor visits
options.B: Small changes in condition can rapidly lead to major health crises
options.C: Clients with brain injuries usually refuse all oral medications
options.D: Nervous system tissues heal completely within a few hours

explanation: Because the central nervous system controls vital functions, even tiny changes in behavior or alertness can signal a dangerous decline. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h1)

question: What three areas does the Glasgow Coma Scale evaluate?

options.A: Eye opening, verbal response, and motor response
options.B: Swallowing ability, skin tone, and pain level
options.C: Temperature, urine output, and bowel sounds
options.D: Heart rate, breathing rate, and blood pressure

explanation: The GCS scores a client based on how they open their eyes, what they say when they talk, and how their body moves. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h2)

question: A client suddenly shows a change in pupil size and a dropping GCS score. What does this most likely indicate?

options.B: An allergic reaction to hospital food
options.C: A sudden drop in body temperature

explanation: Unequal pupils and a worsening level of consciousness are classic warning signs that intracranial pressure is increasing dangerously. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h2)

question: Which nursing diagnosis focuses directly on blood supply to the brain tissue?
explanation: You've got this! This diagnosis simply points to situations where blood and oxygen aren't reaching brain cells properly because of swelling, clots, or bleeding. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h3)

question: Why is Ineffective Airway Clearance such a common worry after a stroke?

options.A: Stroke damage directly destroys the lung tissue and air sacs
options.B: Clients are forced to lie flat on their stomachs all day
options.C: Clients often have a reduced level of consciousness and weak swallowing
options.D: The body produces excessive sweat that blocks the windpipe

explanation: Think about it like this: when brain function drops, natural protective reflexes like coughing and swallowing take a break, making it super easy for spit or mucus to block the airway. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h3)

question: What is the normal range for intracranial pressure in adults?
explanation: Normal ICP is low, ranging between 5 and 15 mmHg. Anything persistently higher requires immediate medical and nursing intervention. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h4)

question: Why should you keep a client's neck straight and in a neutral position when managing high ICP?

options.A: Straight necks make it easier for the client to chew their meals
options.B: It keeps the breathing tube securely taped to the side of the mouth
options.C: It prevents the client from accidentally pulling out their intravenous lines
options.D: Bending the neck can kink jugular veins and trap blood in the head

explanation: Great to know for clinicals! Twisting or bending the neck blocks blood from draining out of the brain, causing it to back up and shoot up the intracranial pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h4)

question: What physical sign on a head bandage might make you suspect a leak of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)?

options.A: A foul-smelling green discharge with pus
options.B: Complete dryness with no visible fluid stains
options.C: Bright red blood soaking through the entire bandage
options.D: A clear yellow halo surrounding a spot of blood

explanation: CSF mixed with blood is clever—it separates on dressings, forming that distinct watery ring or halo right around the blood spot! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h5)

question: Why is keeping a close eye on blood pressure so important right after brain surgery?

options.A: High blood pressure can rupture newly repaired blood vessels or cause bleeding
options.B: Low blood pressure helps the surgical skin incision heal faster
options.C: Fluctuating pressure prevents the client from waking up from anesthesia
options.D: Blood pressure medications replace the need for neurological checks

explanation: Surgical repairs inside the head are super delicate. Sudden spikes in blood pressure put way too much stress on those fresh suture lines. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h5)

question: How does low blood oxygen (hypoxia) affect an injured or swollen brain?

options.A: It helps the brain rest and heal faster from trauma
options.B: It has no real effect on brain tissue recovery
options.C: It lowers intracranial pressure back to normal levels
options.D: It worsens brain tissue damage and increases swelling

explanation: Oxygen is food for the brain! Starving delicate brain cells of oxygen causes more cells to die and makes the swelling much worse. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h6)

question: What is a golden rule when suctioning airway secretions in a client with high ICP?

options.A: Turn the client flat on their back before starting suction
options.B: Skip pre-oxygenation to save time during the procedure
options.C: Avoid prolonged suctioning because coughing spikes ICP
options.D: Always suction for at least two full minutes to clear all mucus

explanation: Suctioning makes anyone cough and gag, which temporarily shoots up the pressure inside the head. Always keep your passes short and give oxygen first! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h6)

question: What is the main reason nurses use splints and range-of-motion exercises for bedridden clients?

options.A: To cure underlying brain tissue infections
options.C: To eliminate the need for turning the client
options.D: To increase daily urine and stool output

explanation: Moving the joints and positioning them right keeps them flexible and stops muscles from freezing into stiff, awkward positions. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h7)

question: Why must a stroke client pass a swallow test before you give them normal food?

options.A: To check if the client has an allergy to hospital cutlery
options.B: To prevent food from entering the airway and causing aspiration pneumonia
options.C: To ensure the stomach can digest heavy proteins and fats
options.D: To find out which specific food flavors the client prefers to eat

explanation: Stroke weakness can make throat muscles sluggish, meaning food or water can easily slip down the 'wrong pipe' into the lungs instead of the belly. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h7)

question: When should you ideally start planning for a neurological client's discharge?

options.A: Only after all therapy sessions are finished
options.B: The evening before the client goes home
options.C: When the doctor finally writes the discharge order
options.D: On the day of hospital admission

explanation: It sounds early, but starting day one gives you enough breathing room to sort out equipment, teach family members, and prep the home before discharge day sneaks up! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h8)

question: Why is teaching the family so important before sending a neuro client home?

options.A: Clients with brain injuries never regain their memory or thinking skills
options.B: Family members are legally required to pass a written nursing exam
options.C: Caregivers need to recognize warning signs of complications and manage daily care
options.D: Home health nurses are not allowed to visit clients after discharge

explanation: Since family members will be doing the heavy lifting at home, they need to know what red flags mean it's time to rush back to the hospital. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T21#GNS222_U3_T21_h8)
